hero.headline: Spirit Airlines bankruptcy puts Treasure Coast entrepreneur's $250 million bid in spotlight
hero.teaser: A Treasure Coast entrepreneur has proposed buying all of Spirit Airlines and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach, as the carrier enters bankruptcy court.
hero.body:
LeRoy Gillead II, a Treasure Coast entrepreneur, has submitted a proposal to purchase Spirit Airlines in its entirety, rehire its workforce, and rebrand the carrier as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach. According to court documents, Gillead is attempting to secure up to $250 million from private investors to fund the acquisition. The deadline for all bids is scheduled for July.

Spirit Airlines is currently in bankruptcy court liquidating its assets, which include aircraft, airport gates, and potentially its headquarters. These physical assets represent significant value in the aviation industry. The airline's closure removes another budget-friendly option for cost-conscious travelers at a time when airfare prices remain high. Many passengers relied on Spirit's low fares to make air travel affordable.

Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed skepticism about Gillead's proposal becoming reality. "This seems like a pie in the sky thing," Henderson said. While acknowledging that money could potentially be raised to establish a new low-cost carrier, he noted that such an operation currently has no routes or operational infrastructure. Henderson believes it is far more probable that Spirit's assets will be distributed among multiple bidders, likely major airlines. Those major carriers would acquire the valuable planes and gates rather than seeing them consolidated under a single new operator.

The disappearance of Spirit Airlines reflects a larger trend affecting the budget airline sector. Henderson noted that low-cost carriers are struggling nationwide, with the business model facing significant challenges. Only Frontier and Allegiant remain operating in the true low-cost category. For travelers seeking affordable fares, Henderson recommends a flexible approach. "Be airline agnostic," he advised consumers. "Go with the cheapest airline you can find. Use Google Flights and don't try to be loyal to one airline." This strategy requires more effort to find bargains but offers the best chance of securing discounted tickets in the current market. The iconic yellow aircraft Spirit was known for will likely be repainted and operated under different airline brands if purchased by larger carriers.

cards.headline: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to end temporary protected status for Haiti, Syria migrants
cards.body:
The Supreme Court voted 6-3 to allow the Trump administration to end temporary protected status for migrants from Haiti and Syria, clearing the way for potential deportations of hundreds of thousands of people. The decision overturned lower court orders blocking the Department of Homeland Security from ending the program, which currently protects 1.3 million people from 17 countries. The conservative majority ruled that immigration authorities have sole control over the program and that judges cannot intervene in such decisions. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor dissented. This marks the second immigration policy victory for President Trump at the high court this week, following a decision that allows revival of restrictions on asylum seekers.

Florida politicians responded quickly and sharply to the ruling. Governor Ron DeSantis called it a correct decision, arguing that the three liberal justices believed temporary status was essentially permanent. U.S. Representatives Maxwell Frost, Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz all opposed the decision. Frost said it will devastate families, communities and the country. Moskowitz warned that deporting Haitian TPS holders to a nation the State Department considers too dangerous to visit will create severe economic consequences. Wasserman Schultz called the decision despicable and announced plans to introduce legislation to reverse it, noting that hundreds of thousands of families who followed all legal requirements and paid taxes now face separation and deportation. Florida House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell said TPS recipients work legally, pay taxes and raise families, and are now uncertain whether America's promise still applies to them.

Miami-Dade Commissioner Marleine Bastien, who previously ran a nonprofit assisting the Haitian community, warned that hundreds of thousands of jobs could become vacant in healthcare, hospitality, construction, manufacturing and business services. She emphasized that Haiti remains in crisis with extreme violence and instability, making forced returns unconscionable. Commissioner Oliver Gilbert characterized Trump's motivation as patently racist, while former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness called the decision legally reckless and morally bankrupt. State Rep. Angie Nixon, a Senate candidate, said the ruling puts millions of lives into uncertainty and fear. Senate candidate Alex Vindman described it as a broken promise to thousands of immigrants who built lives and contributed to Florida communities while waiting for conditions to improve in their home countries.

cards.headline: Stuart man crashes into Hobe Sound water plant, leaving 7,000 residents without water service
cards.teaser: A Stuart man crashed into a large pipe at the South Martin Regional Utility's North Water Treatment Plant and fled the scene Wednesday night, leaving about 7,000 residents without water service or adequate water pressure.
cards.body:
A Stuart man crashed into a water pipe at South Martin Regional Utility's North Water Treatment Plant on Wednesday around 9 p.m., causing approximately 7,000 residents to lose water service or experience inadequate water pressure. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, Eliuvar Garza, 24, was speeding when he blew through a stop sign at Osprey Street and Wren Avenue. He then allegedly went through a fence at the water treatment plant, hit a palm tree and broke it in half, then landed on top of the water pipe before fleeing the scene. Hobe Sound resident Mia Coady said her brother rushed to help the driver, but Garza screamed for help and then jumped the fence and ran away.

Deputies found Garza when a family member brought him to the hospital for his injuries. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said Garza was disoriented, reeked of alcohol, and told deputies he had drunk two Corona beers. The sheriff noted that Garza has multiple speeding tickets and has never had a driver's license. SMRU Director Matt Hammond said water utility crews restored service within two hours and issued a boil water notice expected to remain in effect through the weekend. Garza faces charges including leaving the scene of a crash with property damage, driving without a license, failure to use due care, and failure to stop at a stop sign.

cards.headline: Judge sets July 29 hearing for challenge to DeSantis property tax ballot language
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge is fast-tracking a lawsuit that challenges the wording of Gov. Ron DeSantis' property tax amendment before counties begin printing ballots for the General Election.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge Angela Dempsey set a July 29 hearing for a lawsuit challenging the wording of Gov. Ron DeSantis' proposed property tax constitutional amendment. The plaintiffs, a group called Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language joined by former Stuart Mayor Thomas Campenni and former Key Biscayne Mayor Michael Davey, are not asking to remove the amendment entirely but argue that the ballot title and summary mislead voters. They say the ballot summary promises to ensure funding for core services, but the amendment would actually require local governments to spend whatever property tax revenue remains on public safety, schools, infrastructure, and natural resources. The plaintiffs contend that by substantially reducing the local property tax base, the amendment is likely to decrease revenues available to local governments to fund core services.

Lawmakers passed House Joint Resolution 1F during this month's Special Session, putting the measure on the ballot. If at least 60% of voters approve, the amendment would raise the nonschool homestead exemption to $150,000 starting Jan. 1, 2027, and then to $250,000 the following year. It would also cut the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property from 10% to 5%. State analysts estimate the proposal would shrink local property tax collections by almost $5 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year, with yearly impact rising to more than $10.7 billion by 2030-31. DeSantis emphasized the need for quick resolution before counties print ballots for the General Election.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound water service restored after crash at treatment plant, boil water advisory remains in effect
cards.body:
Water service has been restored in Hobe Sound following a vehicle crash at the water treatment facility, though a boil water advisory remains in effect for residents in the area. A man crashed into a pipe at the Hobe Sound water treatment plant, causing damage to critical infrastructure and disrupting water service to customers. The incident forced utility crews to work quickly to restore water pressure and repair the damaged pipe while authorities investigated the crash.

The driver fled the scene immediately after the collision but was later identified and arrested by Martin County authorities. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the man should have never been operating a vehicle at the time of the incident, suggesting there may have been legal or medical reasons preventing him from driving. The exact circumstances surrounding why the driver should not have been behind the wheel were not detailed in available reports. The quick identification and apprehension of the suspect helped authorities begin their investigation into how the crash occurred.

The damage to the water treatment facility required immediate attention from utility crews to restore normal service. Workers assessed the extent of the damage to the pipe and surrounding infrastructure before beginning repairs. Once water service was restored to the area, officials implemented a precautionary boil water advisory for all residents and businesses in Hobe Sound. This advisory requires customers to boil water before drinking or using it for cooking until water quality tests confirm the system is safe for consumption.

Martin County officials continue to evaluate the full scope of damage to the water treatment facility as the investigation progresses. The boil water advisory will remain in place until water samples are tested and analyzed to ensure the water meets safety standards. Residents have been urged to follow the advisory guidelines during this period. Officials have not yet announced when the boil water advisory might be lifted, noting it will depend on the results of ongoing water quality testing and the completion of any additional repairs deemed necessary to the treatment facility.

cards.headline: Thousands of Haitians in Palm Beach County at risk of deportation after Supreme Court eliminates Temporary Protected Status
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. Palm Beach County ranks third nationally with 68,400 Haitian immigrants, according to the Migration Policy Institute.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court has sided with President Donald Trump's administration in eliminating Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. This decision leaves hundreds of thousands suddenly vulnerable to deportation, including many living in South Florida. Temporary Protected Status allows foreign citizens already in the United States to remain, work, and raise families while their home countries face turmoil from natural disasters, political unrest, or violence. For Haitians and Syrians, that protection is now ending.

The Trump administration argues that TPS was designed only as short-term relief during crises and claims conditions in Haiti and Syria have improved enough to no longer justify the protection. Advocates strongly dispute this claim. The administration maintains that the Department of Homeland Security has sole discretion to determine when protections end and that courts should not interfere. Florida has the largest Haitian immigrant population in the United States. Palm Beach County ranks third nationally with 68,400 Haitian immigrants, according to the Migration Policy Institute, behind Miami-Dade County with 78,800 and Broward County with 86,100.

Stecko Dulcio, who owns a restaurant serving Haitian cuisine in Riviera Beach, is a citizen but expresses deep concern for friends with TPS status. He describes Haiti as dangerous, noting that gangs have taken control of houses, transportation, and fuel widespread violence. "That's going to be a disaster," Dulcio said. "Not only are their lives in danger, but even if they go they don't get killed, they're going to have a miserable life, because there's no work, no job, and they lose everything they have." He urged the U.S. government to take action to help affected people.

Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who is Haitian and represents many people losing TPS, explains the practical impact of losing this status. "It means that if you have a job you no longer are able to work, it means that you were once legal and now you have to go in the shadow," Guillaume said. He raises additional concerns for families with American-born children, questioning whether parents would leave their children in the United States or take them to Haiti, a country they have never known. "I do think lives will be at risk," Guillaume said. The ruling affects roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide. Guillaume noted that no timeline on deportations has been set. Since January of last year, DHS has ended protections for people from more than 13 countries.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens new primary care facility in Vero Beach to address Indian River County shortage
cards.teaser: Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam room adult primary care center in Vero Beach located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101. The facility can take 40 patients a day and has opportunity to grow, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The health care center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met during residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City.

Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area by the Cleveland Clinic. Dr. Kristos said the shortage has led to patients waiting months for appointments. Christine Stenback, who moved to Indian River County nearly three decades ago, described the primary care shortage as a longstanding problem. When she first moved with her daughter, there were few primary care physicians and no specialists available, forcing her family to retain doctors in Fort Lauderdale and travel back for care. Dr. Kristos said the new facility aims to provide quick timeframes for patients to get established and offer access when health issues arise, reducing wait times and increasing access to quality health care.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's survival in Venezuela building collapse a miracle
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, spent hours not knowing if his mother survived when her high-rise building collapsed after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of the disaster from news alerts about two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck Venezuela seconds apart. When videos arrived showing the building where his mother lived, Peroza faced hours of uncertainty as communication in Venezuela collapsed along with power and internet connections. About eight hours after the collapse, around 3 a.m., he received a call confirming his mother was alive but trapped under rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to free her. His mother suffered a broken hip, requires surgery, and lost her home in the collapse.

Peroza described a wider humanitarian crisis in the coastal state of La Guaira, where there is no power or water. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are injured. He said Venezuela lacks the structure and equipment to handle a disaster of this scale, with most buildings made of concrete and metal making rescue efforts nearly impossible. Peroza called his mother's survival "absolutely a miracle" and emphasized that Venezuela needs urgent international help. The United States said it will send crews to assist. Peroza said he plans to help his mother from Florida rather than traveling to the disaster zone, believing he can do more good from where there is commercial activity.

cards.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund in Boca Raton awards record $7.5 million to Palm Beach and Broward students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. President Tim Snow said the program is designed to bridge the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford, offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that the fund's services extend beyond financial assistance, providing mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund's expanded services include the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which provides professional, formal, and casual wear to help scholars approach interviews, internships, and campus life with confidence. Donations to the boutique include new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Zoo reveals first-ever koala joey is a boy
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Zoo announced Thursday that their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy, representing a milestone for the zoo and hope for an endangered species.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach Zoo has announced its first-ever koala joey is a boy. Animal Experience Curator Mike Terrell shared the news at the koala habitat, explaining that the joey was born in September no bigger than a jelly bean and immediately crawled into his mother Elin's pouch. The joey is now starting to explore and spends most of his time on his mother's back, usually keeping an arm connected to her for safety as he ventures into the world.

The joey's arrival coincides with the Palm Beach Zoo's unveiling of an expanded koala habitat featuring a climate-controlled indoor forest with solar tubes for natural lighting and carefully designed perching areas that encourage natural behaviors. The joey is part of a critical conservation program facilitated by San Diego Zoo Global, with koalas in North America on loan from the Australian federal government to support vital conservation efforts. According to Terrell, visitors to the zoo are directly contributing to saving koalas in the wild. As the joey continues to grow more independent, zoo visitors will soon witness him riding on his mother's back, a milestone expected closer to summer.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's survival in Venezuela earthquake a 'miracle'
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother survived when her building collapsed in Venezuela after two powerful earthquakes struck.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods, a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of two powerful earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck his home country seconds apart when news alerts came through. A video sent to him showed the building where his mother was living had collapsed. Hours later, his brother confirmed their mother had been inside the building when it collapsed. Communication in Venezuela was severely compromised due to power outages and severed connections, leaving Peroza uncertain about his mother's fate for hours. About eight hours after the collapse, around 3 a.m., he received a call confirming his mother was alive but trapped under the rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to free her. Peroza's mother sustained a broken hip, requires surgery, and lost her home in the collapse.

Peroza described a severe humanitarian crisis in the coastal state of La Guaira, where survivors face no power, no water, and no homes. He said Venezuela lacks the structure and equipment to manage a disaster of this scale and needs international help immediately. The United States has said it will send crews to help. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are hurt. Peroza expressed concern about survivors' immediate needs, noting there is no clear plan for food, work, or shelter in the coming days.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade certifications to residents
cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade is offering programs to get people trained and ready to find work in trades including culinary, welding, and carpentry.
cards.body:
West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade brought a giant truck to a recent Let's Hear It meet-up at the library in Belle Glade to spread the word about their training programs. WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass connected with the people behind the truck and learned about the center's mission to get people trained and ready to find work.

Adrian Dowdell with the education center said West Tech is appropriate for high school students and adults looking to learn a trade and get certifications that lead to work. The center has programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and much more. They also work with community and business partners to help people find work in Belle Glade and surrounding communities.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie approves $1.3 million treatment plan for Sawgrass Lakes water issues
cards.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved funding for a $1.3 million three-year treatment plan for water in the Sawgrass Lakes community stormwater tract using a solution called trymarine.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie city council approved $1.3 million in funding Monday for a three-year treatment plan to address water quality issues in the Sawgrass Lakes community. The city will use a solution called TryMarine and continue working with their vendor SOLitutde to conduct the treatment and test water quality. Kevin Matyjaszek, utility systems director for Port St. Lucie, said the city wants to ensure the chemistry is correct before proceeding. In March, city staff addressed concerns from neighbors, and the community voted to approve the TryMarine approach.

The decision comes weeks after a fish kill wiped out approximately 1,100 fish in the stormwater tract. Bob Shonce, HOA president of North Panther Trace at Sawgrass Lakes, said he and other neighbors have observed changes in the water for over five years. Matyjaszek explained that the stormwater tract has muck and sediment issues that lower oxygen levels and water quality, making it susceptible to algae growth. TryMarine could help reduce the muck and restore oxygen levels. However, Jim Moir, executive director of the Indian Riverkeeper, cautioned that while TryMarine may help reduce sediment, it may not address where the muck originates, and the city needs to examine the underlying issue.

hero.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner says mother's survival in Venezuela earthquake collapse is a miracle
hero.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother survived after being trapped for eight hours under rubble from two powerful earthquakes in Venezuela.
hero.body:
Josney Peroza, who owns and operates Ukelele Foods, a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, learned of a devastating disaster through news alerts reporting two earthquakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck seconds apart in Venezuela. When videos of the collapsed building where his mother lived began circulating, his worst fears intensified. Hours later, his brother confirmed that their mother had been inside the structure when it fell. With power outages and severed connections throughout Venezuela, Peroza spent an agonizing stretch of time unable to reach anyone or confirm whether his mother had survived. About eight hours after the collapse, he finally received a call at 3 a.m. stating that his mother was alive but trapped under the rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to dig her out. His mother sustained a broken hip requiring surgery and lost her home in the disaster.

Peroza describes his food truck as more than just a place to eat. "This is more than a food truck. It is a cultural Venezuelan experience that we share with the community," he said. "We call it Venezuela without a passport." The broader humanitarian crisis extends far beyond his family's tragedy. The coastal state of La Guaira and surrounding areas now face critical shortages of power and water, leaving thousands homeless. Officials confirm nearly 200 people have died and at least 1,000 others have been injured. Peroza emphasized that Venezuela lacks the infrastructure and resources to handle a disaster of this magnitude, calling for immediate international assistance. The United States has committed to sending rescue crews to support recovery efforts.

Peroza highlighted the challenges facing rescue workers operating in the disaster zone. Most buildings in the area are constructed from concrete and metal, making rescue efforts extremely difficult without proper equipment. "How can you help with your bare hands?" he asked, noting that residents are forced to rely on faith and prayer while awaiting international support. When asked if he considers his mother's survival a miracle, Peroza responded without hesitation: "Yeah, it's absolutely a miracle." He expressed deep concern for the thousands of other survivors facing similar circumstances, describing the building where his mother lived as having 12 to 15 floors that likely housed about 100 families.

Rather than traveling to Venezuela, Peroza believes he can provide more meaningful assistance from Florida. With no commercial activity expected in the coming days and limited employment opportunities, he plans to help his mother secure housing from afar. He intends to continue operating his food truck while working to support his country's recovery. "I believe this is part of our culture, get over the circumstances, and I think this is the way we can help," Peroza said. "We pray for Venezuela, but we work for Venezuela too, because it's not about my mom, it's no longer about us, it's about our people down there."

cards.headline: Breeze Airways adds five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport starting at $79
cards.teaser: Treasure Coast travelers will have five new destination options from Vero Beach Regional Airport when Breeze Airways launches routes to Atlantic City, Baltimore, Burlington, Provo and Trenton this fall.
cards.body:
Breeze Airways announced five new routes from Vero Beach Regional Airport with one-way fares starting at $79. Travelers can book nonstop flights to Atlantic City, New Jersey on Mondays and Fridays starting October 2 from $89 one way, and to Baltimore on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays starting October 1 from $79 one way. Nonstop service to Trenton, New Jersey begins September 30 on Wednesdays and Saturdays, switching to Thursdays and Sundays beginning January 7, with fares from $89 one way.

Breeze will also offer one-stop, no-change-of-plane BreezeThru service to Burlington, Vermont on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Sundays starting October 4, and to Provo, Utah on Mondays, Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays starting October 2. Breeze, which started operations in 2021, currently operates more than 300 year-round and seasonal routes to 91 cities in the United States, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. The new service comes as Vero Beach Regional Airport has seen dramatic growth in passenger numbers over the past year. JetBlue began service to Boston and New York's JFK airports in December, and American Airlines began service to Charlotte in February.

cards.headline: South Fork High School football welcomes new head coach Eric Kresser for fall season
cards.teaser: South Fork High School's football team is back in summer workouts in Stuart as the Bulldogs prepare for the upcoming fall season under new head coach Eric Kress.
cards.body:
South Fork High School's football team is back in summer workouts in Stuart as the Bulldogs prepare for the upcoming fall season under new head coach Eric Kresser. Kresser, who previously served as head coach at The Benjamin School, has taken over a program that hasn't had a winning season since 2015. The team is currently engaged in summer conditioning and participating in 7 on 7 tournaments. "I'm really excited about what I'm seeing," Kresser said. He emphasized the importance of meeting time and learning football fundamentals to turn the program around. "Where there's a will, there's a way, as they say, and there's a lot of will here," Kresser said.

Senior Jaahad Henry said the team is energized heading into the season and believes the new coaching staff is the key to a quick turnaround. "We have a lot of great guys out here. We have some great coaches, a lot of great coaches and we're going to have a great season this year," Henry said. He expressed excitement about playing football, saying "let's get through it and play some football, man." The Bulldogs are set to begin the season in August.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Zoo reveals first-ever koala joey is a boy
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Zoo announced their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy, marking a monumental milestone for the West Palm Beach facility.
cards.body:
Animal Experience Curator Mike Terrell announced at a gender reveal at the koala habitat that the Palm Beach Zoo's first-ever koala joey is a boy. Born in September no bigger than a jelly bean, the joey immediately crawled into his mother Elin's pouch where he has been growing and developing for months. Terrell said the joey is starting to explore and spends most of his time on his mother's back, usually keeping an arm connected to her for safety as he grows more independent each day.

The Palm Beach Zoo has unveiled an expanded koala habitat featuring a climate-controlled indoor forest with solar tubes for natural lighting and carefully designed perching areas that encourage natural behaviors. As part of a critical conservation program facilitated by San Diego Zoo Global, koalas in North America are on loan from the Australian federal government to support vital conservation efforts. Terrell emphasized that visitors help save wild koalas simply by visiting the zoo, making each guest a participant in the conservation mission for this endangered species.

cards.headline: Boca Raton George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund headquartered in Boca Raton has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded a record $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. President Tim Snow said the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that the fund's services extend beyond financial assistance, providing mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate planning to attend Georgetown University, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, offers professional, formal, and casual wear to help scholars prepare for interviews, internships, and campus life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories.

cards.headline: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade offers trade certifications to local residents
cards.teaser: West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade is spreading the word about programs to get people trained and ready to find work through trade certifications.
cards.body:
WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass recently connected with the team at West Technical Education Center in Belle Glade at a Let's Hear It meet-up held at the library. The education center had brought a large truck to the event to promote their training programs and employment opportunities for local residents. Adrian Dowdell with the education center explained that West Tech serves high school students and adults seeking to learn a trade and earn certifications that lead to work.

West Tech offers programs in culinary, welding, carpentry and other trades. The center works with community and business partners to help residents find employment in Belle Glade and surrounding communities. The programs provide hands-on training that leads to industry certifications and jobs for people in the Belle Glade area.

cards.headline: Royal Palm Beach and Wellington clean up after strong storms topple trees and damage property
cards.teaser: Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles across both communities.
cards.body:
Strong thunderstorms swept through Royal Palm Beach and Wellington Wednesday night, toppling trees, twisting fences and knocking down light poles. In one Royal Palm Beach neighborhood, a large tree was uprooted and fell into the road, blocking traffic. Firefighters responded and pulled the tree from the road so neighbors could clear it. Hail pelted cars, lightning struck close to residents and strong winds caused widespread damage throughout the area.

Seven-year-old Danny Jaworski was home with his grandmother when the storm hit. "I heard a cracking sound and then a boom," Danny said. He and his grandmother watched as the massive tree came down in front of a car driving down their street. Danny's mother, Leslie Jaworski, owns the home, which had been named the neighborhood's Home of the Month. She was at work when the storm hit and came home to find firefighters already on scene working to clear the tree. "I was grateful that the tree didn't go this way and land on my roof, because I've heard horror stories of that," Leslie said. As a new homeowner, the experience left her thinking about future storms. "It kind of blew my mind," she said.

hero.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 Palm Beach, Broward students
hero.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, has achieved a record-breaking milestone in 2026, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties.
hero.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund has announced a major achievement, awarding more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026. According to President Tim Snow, who spoke with WPTV, this record-breaking distribution reflects the nonprofit's continued expansion of financial and educational support for students in South Florida.

Since its founding over 40 years ago, GSSF has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, establishing itself as the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. Snow explained that the program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can actually afford to pay. The nonprofit's approach includes four-year scholarship commitments that provide stability and predictability as students work through their college education. Beyond monetary assistance, Vice President of Development Jay Brandt noted that GSSF offers mentorship, professional development opportunities, and educational resources including the College Compass podcast to help scholars succeed both academically and professionally.

One recipient benefiting from the fund's support is Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate heading to Georgetown University. Chow earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship. Her selection highlights how GSSF's diverse funding sources allow the organization to support students with varying backgrounds and circumstances.

The scholarship fund has also expanded its services beyond financial aid. The Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, provides professional, formal, and casual clothing to help students prepare for interviews, internships, and college life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories from the community. This comprehensive approach to student support reflects GSSF's understanding that removing barriers to success involves more than tuition assistance. As higher education costs continue to rise across the nation, organizations like the George Snow Scholarship Fund play an increasingly important role in making college accessible to underserved students in South Florida.

cards.headline: Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League urges South Florida pet owners to prepare hurricane plans
cards.teaser: With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits.
cards.body:
With hurricane season in full swing, Peggy Adams Animal Rescue League is urging South Florida residents to create a disaster plan for their pets before the next storm hits. Dr. Alyssa Comroe, CEO of Peggy Adams, told WPTV the safest place for pets during a hurricane is right alongside their owners. The shelter's expert team recommends several key steps for pet safety, including ensuring pets wear a collar with current identification and have an updated microchip registered with correct contact information. Pet owners should introduce pets to a designated safe room ahead of time, such as a walk-in closet or downstairs bathroom, and conduct practice runs so the hurricane isn't their first time there.

Pet owners should prepare an emergency kit with a three-day supply of food and water in airtight containers, bowls, a sturdy carrier, bedding, towels, medications for two weeks, vaccination records, first-aid supplies, litter and box for cats, leashes, harnesses, cool packs, wipes, waste bags, and multiple forms of visible ID. Organizers recommend keeping a printed list of local pet-friendly shelters and hotels in an accessible place and maintaining recent photos of pets, ideally with their owner, to help with identification if separated. Conducting hurricane drills that include pets' daily routines, such as feeding, drinking water, and resting inside the safe room, can maximize comfort later. Florida's hurricane season runs June through November, overlapping with extreme summer heat.

cards.headline: Florida Mango Festival Saturday in West Palm Beach features 75 vendors, rare varieties
cards.teaser: Florida-grown mangoes from sweet and creamy to citrusy and tropical will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beac.
cards.body:
Florida-grown mangoes from sweet and creamy to citrusy and tropical will take center stage Saturday, June 27, at the Florida Mango Festival inside the Palm Beach County Convention Center. Organizers said the event will feature more than 75 vendors serving up local mango varieties, grafted trees, tropical fruits, and mango-themed products. Alex Salazar of Tropical Acres Farms told WPTV's T.A. Walker that the indoor, air-conditioned venue offers an ideal setting for people to taste, learn, and discover the magic of Florida-grown mangoes without worrying about the summer heat.

Festival co-organizer Vince Rogers previewed some of the state's most unique varieties, including Fruit Cocktail, a sweet, multi-layered flavor; Orange Sherbet, offering creamy citrus notes; and Pineapple Pleasure, with tropical pineapple undertones. He said Florida hosts more than 350 mango varieties far beyond what's typically available in grocery stores. Throughout the day, visitors can attend educational talks on home mango growing and grafting techniques. Salazar will lead demonstrations, offering tips to ensure success for both beginners and seasoned growers. Additional features include an ID Your Mango booth, a scion exchange for online mango community members, and a master display of Florida's diverse mango cultivars. The festival takes place Saturday, June 27, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. at the Palm Beach County Convention Center, 650 Okeechobee Blvd., West Palm Beach.

hero.headline: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to end temporary protected status for Haiti, Syria migrants
hero.body:
The Supreme Court voted 6-3 to allow the Trump administration to end temporary protected status for migrants from Haiti and Syria, clearing the way for potential deportations of hundreds of thousands of people. The decision overturned lower court orders blocking the Department of Homeland Security from ending the program, which currently protects 1.3 million people from 17 countries. The conservative majority ruled that immigration authorities have sole control over the program and that judges cannot intervene in such decisions. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor dissented. This marks the second immigration policy victory for President Trump at the high court this week, following a decision that allows revival of restrictions on asylum seekers.

Florida politicians responded quickly and sharply to the ruling. Governor Ron DeSantis called it a correct decision, arguing that the three liberal justices believed temporary status was essentially permanent. U.S. Representatives Maxwell Frost, Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz all opposed the decision. Frost said it will devastate families, communities and the country. Moskowitz warned that deporting Haitian TPS holders to a nation the State Department considers too dangerous to visit will create severe economic consequences. Wasserman Schultz called the decision despicable and announced plans to introduce legislation to reverse it, noting that hundreds of thousands of families who followed all legal requirements and paid taxes now face separation and deportation. Florida House Democratic Leader Fentrice Driskell said TPS recipients work legally, pay taxes and raise families, and are now uncertain whether America's promise still applies to them.

Miami-Dade Commissioner Marleine Bastien, who previously ran a nonprofit assisting the Haitian community, warned that hundreds of thousands of jobs could become vacant in healthcare, hospitality, construction, manufacturing and business services. She emphasized that Haiti remains in crisis with extreme violence and instability, making forced returns unconscionable. Commissioner Oliver Gilbert characterized Trump's motivation as patently racist, while former Broward County Mayor Dale Holness called the decision legally reckless and morally bankrupt. State Rep. Angie Nixon, a Senate candidate, said the ruling puts millions of lives into uncertainty and fear. Senate candidate Alex Vindman described it as a broken promise to thousands of immigrants who built lives and contributed to Florida communities while waiting for conditions to improve in their home countries.

cards.headline: Judge sets July 29 hearing for challenge to DeSantis property tax ballot language
cards.teaser: A Leon County judge is fast-tracking a lawsuit that challenges the wording of Gov. Ron DeSantis' property tax amendment before counties begin printing ballots for the General Election.
cards.body:
Circuit Judge Angela Dempsey set a July 29 hearing for a lawsuit challenging the wording of Gov. Ron DeSantis' proposed property tax constitutional amendment. The plaintiffs, a group called Save Our Voters From Misleading Ballot Language joined by former Stuart Mayor Thomas Campenni and former Key Biscayne Mayor Michael Davey, are not asking to remove the amendment entirely but argue that the ballot title and summary mislead voters. They say the ballot summary promises to ensure funding for core services, but the amendment would actually require local governments to spend whatever property tax revenue remains on public safety, schools, infrastructure, and natural resources. The plaintiffs contend that by substantially reducing the local property tax base, the amendment is likely to decrease revenues available to local governments to fund core services.

Lawmakers passed House Joint Resolution 1F during this month's Special Session, putting the measure on the ballot. If at least 60% of voters approve, the amendment would raise the nonschool homestead exemption to $150,000 starting Jan. 1, 2027, and then to $250,000 the following year. It would also cut the annual cap on assessment increases for non-homestead property from 10% to 5%. State analysts estimate the proposal would shrink local property tax collections by almost $5 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year, with yearly impact rising to more than $10.7 billion by 2030-31. DeSantis emphasized the need for quick resolution before counties print ballots for the General Election.

cards.headline: Political committee launches campaign against DeSantis property tax amendment
cards.teaser: A political committee chaired by former Leon County Commissioner Bryan Desloge is urging Floridians to reject Amendment 3, warning of higher rent, more expensive purchases, and costlier first homes.
cards.body:
The Stop Unfair Tax Shifts political committee is mounting opposition to Amendment 3, a proposed constitutional amendment that would increase homestead exemptions to $250,000. The committee, chaired by former Leon County Commissioner Bryan Desloge, argues that the amendment will shift bills for public safety, roads and bridges, stormwater protection and hurricane response to renters, consumers and small business owners. According to the committee, the consequences will include higher rent, more expensive everyday purchases, costlier first homes, and pressure on small businesses unable to absorb increases in commercial property taxes.

If approved by at least 60% of voters in November, the amendment would lift homestead exemptions for primary residence owners to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with further increases tied to the consumer price index. School taxes would be exempted. Newer residents would qualify for a $50,000 exemption initially, reaching full benefit after five years. The Office of Economic and Demographic Research estimates $11.86 billion would eventually be extracted from local budgets annually. St. Lucie County faces the steepest impact with a projected 35% revenue loss, while Miami-Dade would lose $445 million, Hillsborough $353 million, Broward $326 million, Duval $277 million, and Orange $253 million by Fiscal Year 2028-29.

cards.headline: Attorney General announces arrest in teacher certification exam fraud scheme
cards.teaser: A Broward County woman faces up to 15 years in prison for allegedly taking Florida teacher certification exams on behalf of multiple clients seeking jobs with Broward County Public Schools.
cards.body:
Attorney General James Uthmeier announced the arrest of Kashaundra Knowles, 37, of Fort Lauderdale, accused of orchestrating a proxy-testing scheme that allowed aspiring teachers to obtain passing scores on Florida certification exams fraudulently. According to the Attorney General's Office, Knowles impersonated multiple individuals while taking the Florida Teacher Certification Examinations and other professional exams on behalf of clients. Several of those clients were employed by or seeking jobs with Broward County Public Schools. Uthmeier stated, "If you try to cheat your way into Florida's classrooms, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will hold you accountable."

The investigation began as part of a separate probe into alleged cheating on the NCLEX-RN nursing licensure exam. Pearson VUE investigators identified Knowles after she allegedly appeared in check-in photographs for a nursing exam taken under another person's name in December 2024. Investigators linked Knowles to multiple teacher certification exams through palm-vein biometric data, check-in photographs, surveillance footage, phone records and text messages. Knowles had previously taken a legitimate FTCE exam in 2018, providing investigators with the biometric baseline used to identify her in subsequent proxy-testing attempts. She was arrested on charges of Organized Scheme to Defraud, Unlawful Use of a Two-Way Communication Device and Money Laundering. If convicted, she faces up to 15 years in prison. The investigation remains ongoing, with additional arrests expected.

cards.headline: DCCC criticizes Maria Salazar for touting housing bill support after missing vote
cards.teaser: The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee blasted Rep. Maria Salazar for celebrating passage of a bipartisan housing bill she did not vote for, though her office said she missed the vote due to her mother's death.
cards.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar celebrated passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which cleared the House on a 358-32 vote, posting on Facebook that housing costs are one of the biggest concerns she hears about in South Florida and that she supported the bipartisan legislation. However, Salazar missed the vote, prompting the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee to quickly respond. DCCC spokesperson Madison Andrus said if Salazar is misleading her constituents and taking credit for votes she could not be bothered to show up for, then Miamians will replace her with a real leader who will fight for their ability to afford housing for their families.

Salazar missed the vote and all votes cast that week because of her mother's death. Her office provided a statement saying she has consistently supported the legislation throughout the legislative process, voting for the bill in the House Financial Services Committee and twice on the House floor to advance it to the Senate. The final package includes her RESIDE Act, the Revitalizing Empty Structures Into Desirable Environments Act, which she originally released in September and represents one of her signature housing priorities. President Donald Trump was expected to sign the legislation at an event on Capitol Hill but canceled it amid a fight with the Senate over an election reform bill. The DCCC last year identified Salazar's seat among Florida's Districts in Play for the 2026 election cycle.

cards.headline: Eight Broward leaders endorse Pia Dandiya in Congressional District 22 race
cards.teaser: Former State Rep. Robin Bartleman, County Commissioner Beam Furr, and six other Broward elected officials and community figures announced their support for Pia Dandiya's congressional campaign.
cards.body:
Democratic candidate Pia Dandiya announced endorsements from eight additional Broward elected officials and community figures in her race for Florida's 22nd Congressional District. The new endorsers include Robin Bartleman and Mitch Rosenwald, County Commissioner Beam Furr, School Board Chair Sarah Leonardi, Davie Mayor Judy Paul, Oakland Park Commissioner Fitz Budhoo, Dolphin Democrats President Alfredo Olvera and Democratic Caribbean Caucus member Stewart Webster. School Board Chair Leonardi, a teacher by trade, said Dandiya has "the intelligence, integrity, and work ethic we need in Washington" and will be a strong advocate for the community. Bartleman cited education and institutional concerns, stating "Republicans have spent years attacking public education, undermining our institutions, and putting partisan politics ahead of working families." She said Dandiya is focused on bringing people together, protecting freedoms, and delivering results for communities.

The endorsements build on earlier rounds of support from Broward Mayor Mark Bogen, County Commissioners Nan Rich and Steve Geller, several municipal mayors, U.S. Representatives Lois Frankel and Jill Tokuda, former U.S. Secretary of Education Arne Duncan, and former U.S. Representatives Annie Kuster and Patrick Murphy. Organizations backing Dandiya include Aspire PAC, EMILY's List, Vote Mama and the AAPI Victory Fund. A former high school principal and White House fellow, Dandiya shifted to CD 22 in May after the new congressional map's ratification. She entered the race with more than $1.57 million raised and $1.17 million cash on hand. CD 22 runs from Marco Island to western portions of Palm Beach and Broward counties, with 54.6 percent supporting Trump in 2024.

cards.headline: Rep. Jared Moskowitz hosts fourth annual Sneaker Day on Capitol Hill
cards.teaser: The Parkland Democrat brought together members of Congress and footwear industry leaders to discuss the significance of sneakers to American culture and the economy, despite initial resistance to wearing them in the halls of Congress.
cards.body:
U.S. Rep. Jared Moskowitz, a Parkland Democrat, hosted the fourth annual Sneaker Day on the Hill, an event featuring panel discussions on the significance of the footwear industry to American culture and the economy. Moskowitz acknowledged facing resistance to wearing sneakers in Congress, saying people were offended when he first started the practice, claiming it hurt decorum. "Based on some of the things that get said around here, I don't think decorum is really our problem," Moskowitz said. Speeches were delivered by Moskowitz, wearing Union LA Air Jordan 4 shoes, and U.S. Rep. Sharice Davids, a Kansas Democrat and founder of the World Cup Caucus. Her participation led to displays of special soccer cleats and historic Adidas shoes, including a pair designed for Run DMC and the first Adidas sneakers equipped with step counters.

Pensole Footwear Design Academy founder D'Wayne Edwards, designer of multiple Nike Air Jordans, discussed how sneakers transformed his life, sharing his journey from clerk to designer after submitting shoe designs to L.A. Gear's suggestion box. SOLEcial Studies CommUNITY Academy co-founder Sean Williams advocated for sneakers as vital self-expression. Andy Polk of the Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America noted that shoes can foster understanding in tense political environments. Moskowitz explained his personal connection to sneakers, stemming from memories of his late father taking him to the mall when Air Jordans were released. He wears them in the Capitol to show individuality and honor those memories.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound water service restored after crash at treatment plant, boil water advisory remains in effect
hero.body:
Water service has been restored in Hobe Sound following a vehicle crash at the water treatment facility, though a boil water advisory remains in effect for residents in the area. A man crashed into a pipe at the Hobe Sound water treatment plant, causing damage to critical infrastructure and disrupting water service to customers. The incident forced utility crews to work quickly to restore water pressure and repair the damaged pipe while authorities investigated the crash.

The driver fled the scene immediately after the collision but was later identified and arrested by Martin County authorities. According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the man should have never been operating a vehicle at the time of the incident, suggesting there may have been legal or medical reasons preventing him from driving. The exact circumstances surrounding why the driver should not have been behind the wheel were not detailed in available reports. The quick identification and apprehension of the suspect helped authorities begin their investigation into how the crash occurred.

The damage to the water treatment facility required immediate attention from utility crews to restore normal service. Workers assessed the extent of the damage to the pipe and surrounding infrastructure before beginning repairs. Once water service was restored to the area, officials implemented a precautionary boil water advisory for all residents and businesses in Hobe Sound. This advisory requires customers to boil water before drinking or using it for cooking until water quality tests confirm the system is safe for consumption.

Martin County officials continue to evaluate the full scope of damage to the water treatment facility as the investigation progresses. The boil water advisory will remain in place until water samples are tested and analyzed to ensure the water meets safety standards. Residents have been urged to follow the advisory guidelines during this period. Officials have not yet announced when the boil water advisory might be lifted, noting it will depend on the results of ongoing water quality testing and the completion of any additional repairs deemed necessary to the treatment facility.

cards.headline: Stuart man arrested on 40 counts of child pornography possession
cards.teaser: A Stuart man faces 40 counts of child pornography possession after being arrested again by Martin County authorities.
cards.body:
A Stuart man has been arrested and faces 40 counts of child pornography possession, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The arrest marks the second time the man has been taken into custody on similar charges.

Martin County deputies conducted an investigation that led to the man's arrest. The charges involve possession of images and materials depicting child sexual abuse. The suspect is being held in the Martin County jail pending court proceedings.

cards.headline: SUV flips in Stuart crash, one person hospitalized
cards.teaser: An SUV flipped over after crashing into a parked car in Stuart, sending one person to the hospital.
cards.body:
An SUV overturned in Stuart after colliding with a parked car, resulting in one person being transported to the hospital. The crash occurred Thursday and required emergency medical response to the scene.

Stuart police responded to the accident and worked to clear the roadway. The condition of the injured person was not immediately disclosed. Authorities are investigating the circumstances that led to the vehicle striking the parked car and flipping over.

cards.headline: Martin County staff address concerns over $73 million operations facility
cards.teaser: Martin County staff answered questions about a proposed $73 million operations facility as concerns mount over the project's cost and scope.
cards.body:
Martin County staff addressed public concerns regarding a planned $73 million operations facility during a recent meeting. The facility has drawn attention from residents and officials questioning the scale and expense of the project.

County staff presented details about the operations center and responded to questions about its necessity and budget. The facility is intended to consolidate county operations and improve service delivery. Martin County officials continue to review the project as part of the county's long-term infrastructure planning.

cards.headline: First United Methodist Church of Stuart welcomes new senior pastor
cards.teaser: First United Methodist Church of Stuart has appointed a new senior pastor to lead the congregation.
cards.body:
First United Methodist Church of Stuart has a new senior pastor. The church announced the appointment this week as the new pastor takes over leadership of the congregation.

The pastoral change comes as part of the regular appointment process within the United Methodist Church. The new senior pastor will oversee worship services, church programming, and community outreach efforts. First United Methodist Church of Stuart serves as a longtime fixture in the Martin County faith community.

cards.headline: Man identified in Martin County water plant crash after fleeing scene
cards.teaser: Authorities have identified the man who crashed into a Martin County water plant and fled the scene, causing service disruptions.
cards.body:
The man responsible for crashing into a Martin County water treatment plant has been identified after fleeing the scene. The crash caused significant disruptions to water service in the Hobe Sound area.

Martin County Sheriff's Office deputies located and arrested the driver after he left the crash site. The incident damaged a pipe at the treatment facility, forcing emergency repairs and a boil water advisory. Authorities stated the man should not have been driving at the time of the crash.

cards.headline: Man arrested after crashing into Hobe Sound water treatment pipe
cards.teaser: A man was arrested after crashing his vehicle into a pipe at the Hobe Sound water treatment facility, disrupting service.
cards.body:
A man has been arrested after crashing into a water treatment pipe in Hobe Sound, causing damage to the facility and water service interruptions. The crash occurred at the Hobe Sound water treatment plant and required emergency response from Martin County authorities.

The driver's vehicle struck a critical pipe at the facility, causing water pressure issues and service disruptions for customers. The man was taken into custody by the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Utility crews worked to repair the damaged infrastructure and restore normal water service to affected areas.

hero.headline: Thousands of Haitians in Palm Beach County at risk of deportation after Supreme Court eliminates Temporary Protected Status
hero.teaser: The Supreme Court sided with the Trump administration to eliminate Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. Palm Beach County ranks third nationally with 68,400 Haitian immigrants, according to the Migration Policy Institute.
hero.body:
The Supreme Court has sided with President Donald Trump's administration in eliminating Temporary Protected Status for thousands of people from Haiti and Syria. This decision leaves hundreds of thousands suddenly vulnerable to deportation, including many living in South Florida. Temporary Protected Status allows foreign citizens already in the United States to remain, work, and raise families while their home countries face turmoil from natural disasters, political unrest, or violence. For Haitians and Syrians, that protection is now ending.

The Trump administration argues that TPS was designed only as short-term relief during crises and claims conditions in Haiti and Syria have improved enough to no longer justify the protection. Advocates strongly dispute this claim. The administration maintains that the Department of Homeland Security has sole discretion to determine when protections end and that courts should not interfere. Florida has the largest Haitian immigrant population in the United States. Palm Beach County ranks third nationally with 68,400 Haitian immigrants, according to the Migration Policy Institute, behind Miami-Dade County with 78,800 and Broward County with 86,100.

Stecko Dulcio, who owns a restaurant serving Haitian cuisine in Riviera Beach, is a citizen but expresses deep concern for friends with TPS status. He describes Haiti as dangerous, noting that gangs have taken control of houses, transportation, and fuel widespread violence. "That's going to be a disaster," Dulcio said. "Not only are their lives in danger, but even if they go they don't get killed, they're going to have a miserable life, because there's no work, no job, and they lose everything they have." He urged the U.S. government to take action to help affected people.

Attorney Byrnes Guillaume, who is Haitian and represents many people losing TPS, explains the practical impact of losing this status. "It means that if you have a job you no longer are able to work, it means that you were once legal and now you have to go in the shadow," Guillaume said. He raises additional concerns for families with American-born children, questioning whether parents would leave their children in the United States or take them to Haiti, a country they have never known. "I do think lives will be at risk," Guillaume said. The ruling affects roughly 350,000 Haitians and 6,000 Syrians nationwide. Guillaume noted that no timeline on deportations has been set. Since January of last year, DHS has ended protections for people from more than 13 countries.

cards.headline: Orlando Health opens eight-exam-room primary care center in Vero Beach to address physician shortage
cards.teaser: Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam-room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach.
cards.body:
Orlando Health held a ribbon cutting Thursday for a new eight-exam-room adult primary health care center in Vero Beach, located at 3745 11th Circle Suite 101. The facility can take 40 patients a day and has opportunity to grow, according to Aaron Bridges, assistant vice president of Orlando Health. The center will be led by husband-and-wife physicians Dr. Meron Kristos and Dr. Gabitto, who met in residency at the former St. Vincent's hospital in New York City. Staff told WPTV they hope the new facility can help reduce long wait times and address primary care shortages in Indian River County.

According to the Cleveland Clinic, Indian River County is designated a health professional shortage area and medically underserved area. Kristos said patients are waiting months for primary care appointments. Both physicians noted that primary care access is limited throughout Florida, though the Vero Beach need stood out to them. "We're able to provide as a quick timeframe to see us to get established, and then when something pops up, you have somebody to go see," Kristos said. Long-time resident Christine Stenback, who moved to Indian River County nearly three decades ago, said she and her daughter retained doctors in Fort Lauderdale to access specialist care due to local shortages.

cards.headline: Delray Beach food truck owner calls mother's survival in Venezuela earthquake collapse a miracle
cards.teaser: Josney Peroza, who owns Ukelele Foods and operates a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, said his mother survived after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela and the building where she lived collapsed.
cards.body:
Josney Peroza, owner of Ukelele Foods and a Venezuelan food truck in Delray Beach, is calling his mother's survival after two powerful earthquakes struck Venezuela "absolutely a miracle." Peroza learned of the disaster through news alerts reporting two quakes measuring 7.2 and 7.5 magnitudes that struck seconds apart. When video arrived showing the building where his mother lived, he feared the worst. About eight hours after the collapse, his family received a call confirming she was alive but trapped under rubble. Relatives and neighbors worked with their bare hands to free her. His mother suffered a broken hip requiring surgery and lost her home in the collapse.

Peroza said Venezuela was unprepared for a disaster of this scale, with most buildings made of concrete and metal making rescue efforts nearly impossible with limited tools. Officials confirm nearly 200 people are dead and at least 1,000 others are injured. Peroza expressed concern about survivors' futures, noting there is no clear plan for food, work or shelter. Rather than traveling to Venezuela, he believes he can help more effectively from Florida. "We don't have any plans to go down there. I think that we are more helpful from here," Peroza said.

cards.headline: Treasure Coast entrepreneur proposes buying Spirit Airlines, rebranding as West Palm Beach-based Florida Air Express
cards.teaser: LeRoy Gillead II has proposed buying up all of Spirit Airlines, rehiring the airline's workers and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach.
cards.body:
A Treasure Coast entrepreneur, LeRoy Gillead II, has proposed buying all of Spirit Airlines, rehiring its workers and rebranding it as Florida Air Express, a low-cost airline based in West Palm Beach. Court papers show Gillead is seeking to raise as much as $250 million from private investors. Spirit Airlines is currently in bankruptcy court to sell off all its assets, including planes, airport gates and potentially its headquarters.

Clint Henderson, managing editor of news at The Points Guy travel website, expressed skepticism about the proposal. "This seems like a pie in the sky thing. If they can get the money together, maybe they'll establish a new low-cost carrier, but right now they don't fly any routes at all," Henderson said. He predicted the assets would instead be "divvied out to the highest bidder, and that's probably going to be major airlines." The deadline for bids comes in July. Henderson noted that low-cost carriers are struggling, with Frontier and Allegiant still operating in that category.

cards.headline: Palm Beach Zoo reveals first-ever koala joey is a boy
cards.teaser: The Palm Beach Zoo announced their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy. The joey was born in September no bigger than a jelly bean and has been growing in his mother Elin's pouch for months.
cards.body:
The Palm Beach Zoo announced their first-ever koala joey born on site is a boy. Animal Experience Curator Mike Terrell shared the news at the koala habitat. The joey was born in September no bigger than a jelly bean, immediately crawling into his mother Elin's pouch where he has been growing and developing for months. He is starting to explore a little bit now, Terrell said, spending most of his time on his mother's back while keeping an arm connected to her for safety as he begins to see the world.

The Palm Beach Zoo has just unveiled an expanded koala habitat complete with a climate-controlled indoor forest featuring solar tubes for natural lighting and carefully designed perching areas that encourage natural behaviors. As part of a critical conservation program facilitated by San Diego Zoo Global, koalas in North America are on loan from the Australian federal government to support vital conservation efforts. Terrell emphasized that by visiting the zoo, people are helping to save animals in the wild like these koalas. Zoo visitors will soon witness the joey riding on his mother's back, a milestone expected closer to summer.

cards.headline: Boca Raton's George Snow Scholarship Fund awards record $7.5 million to 470 students in Palm Beach and Broward counties
cards.teaser: The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The program bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford by offering four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college.

Beyond financial assistance, the fund provides mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast, noted Vice President of Development Jay Brandt. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University. The fund's expanded services include the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which offers professional, formal, and casual wear for interviews, internships, and campus life. The boutique accepts donations of new or gently used clothing, footwear, and accessories.
